0.title: Citizens of Heaven, Neighbours on Earth
0.essay:
How should Christians relate to the world around them: to government, politics, culture, neighbours and nation? Christians have answered in very different ways.

Three wrong turns

Some withdraw, building separate communities and keeping their distance from public life. Others try to take over, seeing politics as the main way to advance God’s kingdom. Many simply absorb the values of their culture without noticing.

In the world, not of it

Jesus prayed for his disciples, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world” (John 17:15–16). Christians are citizens of heaven, living for now as “sojourners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11). Yet God calls us to seek the good of the places where we live, to honour those in authority, to do justice and love mercy, and to shine as lights.

Principles and wisdom

This study asks how Christians can live faithfully in public life, neither withdrawing nor being swallowed up. Some of these questions are disputed among faithful Christians, so the study tries to distinguish clear biblical principles from matters of wisdom where believers may differ.

The chapters

Exiles and Citizens; God and Government; When We Must Obey God Rather than Men; Christians and Politics; Salt, Light and Worldliness; and Loving Our Neighbour and Seeking Justice.

For reflection

Which do you lean towards most: withdrawing from the world, trying to control it, or quietly absorbing it?

1.title: Exiles and Citizens
1.essay:
Christians live with a double identity. We are citizens of heaven, and exiles on earth. Yet God sends us into the world to seek its good.

Citizens of heaven

“But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20). Philippi was a Roman colony, and its citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship. Paul tells believers they have a higher one. Their deepest loyalty is to Christ and his kingdom.

Every earthly nation is temporary. That frees us from idolising any country, party or leader. Paul contrasts those “with minds set on earthly things” with those who await a Saviour who will transform their bodies and subject all things to himself (Philippians 3:19–21).

Exiles on earth

Peter writes to believers as “elect exiles” (1 Peter 1:1), and urges them “as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul” (1 Peter 2:11). Exiles live in a land that is not their final home. They are never fully at home in its culture or values. That explains why Christians often feel out of step with the world around them. We are meant to.

Seek the welfare of the city

Yet exile is not withdrawal. When Judah was taken to Babylon, false prophets promised a quick return. God said something very different through Jeremiah: “Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce” (Jeremiah 29:5). And astonishingly: “But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare” (Jeremiah 29:7).

God’s people were to work, marry, raise families and pray for a pagan city, the very city of their enemies. Their good was tied to its good. Christians today are called to the same: to be good neighbours, workers and citizens wherever God has placed them.

Daniel in Babylon

Daniel and his friends were taken to Babylon as young men. They learned its language and literature and served in its government. But they refused to defile themselves with the king’s food or to worship his gods (Daniel 1:8; 3:18). They served the city faithfully without surrendering their loyalty to God.

Good conduct as witness

Peter goes on: “Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12). Christians will be misunderstood and criticised. Our answer is not anger or withdrawal, but consistent goodness, which over time speaks for itself. Inwardly we fight sinful desires; outwardly we live honourably. Holiness and good works are a powerful witness.

Sent

Jesus prayed, “As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world” (John 17:18). Christians are not in the world by accident. We are sent. Every workplace, neighbourhood and nation is a mission field. The Christian life is lived in tension: different from the world, and sent to it.

Think of a Christian family who move to a city where few people go to church. They are tempted either to retreat into a Christian bubble or to blend in quietly. Instead they get to know their neighbours, join a local community group, host street parties and pray for their area. Over the years, several neighbours come to church with them.

Two realms, one Lord

Christians have long distinguished between the spiritual realm, where Christ rules his church by his word and Spirit, and the civil realm, where God rules through governments and common grace. Both belong to God, but they work differently. The church does not wield the sword, and the state does not preach the gospel. Christ is Lord of both.

Common grace

God gives good gifts to all people. “He makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). Family, government, art, science and justice are among his gifts to the whole human race (Acts 14:17). So Christians can appreciate and work alongside unbelievers for the common good, while knowing that only the gospel saves.

Patriotism and its limits

Loving one’s country, praying for it and serving it are good. But patriotism becomes idolatry when national identity is placed above Christ, or when Christians of other nations seem less our brothers and sisters than unbelieving fellow citizens. Our first citizenship is in heaven, and it unites us with believers of every nation.

For reflection

In what ways do you feel like an exile in your culture? Where has God placed you, and what would it look like to seek the welfare of that place this month?

2.title: God and Government
2.essay:
Government is not a human invention or a necessary evil. Scripture calls it God’s servant, given to restrain evil and promote good.

Instituted by God

“Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God” (Romans 13:1). Paul wrote this under Nero, the emperor who would later persecute Christians in Rome. He was not describing an ideal Christian government. He was describing a pagan one, and still calling it God’s servant.

What government is for

Paul explains that the ruler is “God’s servant for your good,” and that “he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). Peter says governors are sent “to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good” (1 Peter 2:14).

Government’s main task is justice: protecting the innocent, punishing wrongdoers and keeping order so that people can live peaceful lives.

What Christians owe

Christians owe government submission, taxes, respect and honour: “Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed” (Romans 13:7). We submit not only to avoid punishment but “for the sake of conscience” (Romans 13:5).

Peter, writing to Christians facing hostility, says, “Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution” (1 Peter 2:13). They are free, but must not use freedom “as a cover-up for evil” (1 Peter 2:16). And he sums up their duties in four short commands: “Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor” (1 Peter 2:17).

That includes obeying laws, paying taxes honestly, and speaking of leaders with respect, even when we disagree with them.

Render to Caesar

When the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus with a question about taxes, he asked whose image was on the coin. Caesar’s. “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21). The coin bears Caesar’s image; we bear God’s. Taxes belong to the government; our whole selves belong to God. Christians should pay their taxes honestly, even when they disagree with how the money is spent.

Pray for those in authority

“First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Paul makes this the church’s first prayer priority. Peace and order make it easier for the gospel to spread, and God “desires all people to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4), rulers included.

Christians should pray regularly for their national and local leaders, by name, including those they did not vote for.

Think of a Christian who strongly dislikes his country’s leader and often speaks of him with contempt online. Reading 1 Timothy 2 and 1 Peter 2, he is convicted. He still disagrees with the leader’s policies, and says so respectfully. But he begins to pray for him by name each week, and stops mocking him.

God rules over rulers

When God revealed the meaning of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, Daniel praised him: “he removes kings and sets up kings” (Daniel 2:21). The most powerful ruler on earth was under God’s hand. So is every ruler today. No one holds power except by God’s permission, and every ruler will answer to him. That gives Christians peace when governments are bad, and humility when governments are good.

Faithful service

God’s people have often served faithfully in governments that did not share their faith. Joseph was second-in-command in Egypt, and through his wise administration saved Egypt and many nations from famine (Genesis 41). Daniel served several kings with integrity. Christians can serve in public office as a calling from God.

Government is limited

Government is God’s servant, not God. It has authority in its own sphere, but not over conscience or the church’s worship and teaching. When government claims divine authority, as Rome did when it demanded emperor worship, it oversteps its role.

And government cannot save. It cannot transform hearts or bring in God’s kingdom. Its role is justice and order. Christians who expect government to do what only the gospel can do will always be disappointed.

For reflection

Why is it significant that Paul wrote Romans 13 under a pagan emperor? How can you honour leaders you disagree with? Make a list of national and local leaders to pray for by name this week.

3.title: When We Must Obey God Rather than Men
3.essay:
Submission to government is the normal Christian duty. But it is not absolute. When human authorities command what God forbids, or forbid what God commands, Christians must obey God.

The apostles’ answer

Peter and John had healed a lame man and preached Christ. The Jewish council ordered them not to speak or teach in Jesus’ name. They answered, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:19–20). It was a model of respectful firmness.

Arrested again, they said simply, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), and then preached the gospel to the council itself. They were beaten. And they left “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41). They did not riot or rebel. They respectfully refused, kept preaching, and accepted the consequences. Obedience to God cost them, but it did not crush their joy.

The midwives

Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill the newborn boys. “But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live” (Exodus 1:17). “So God dealt well with the midwives” (Exodus 1:20). The fear of God gave Shiphrah and Puah courage to defy the most powerful man in the world to protect the vulnerable. Their names are remembered. Pharaoh’s is not.

But if not

Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar’s golden image. Facing the furnace, they said their God was able to deliver them. Then: “But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up” (Daniel 3:18). Their faith did not depend on a guaranteed rescue. It depended on God’s worth.

Daniel, too, kept praying three times a day with his windows open towards Jerusalem, despite the king’s decree (Daniel 6:10).

The pattern

These examples share common features. The command required clear disobedience to God. The believers refused openly, not by deceit where they could avoid it. They were respectful, not contemptuous. They accepted the penalty. And they trusted God with the outcome.

Not every disagreement

Disliking a policy, paying high taxes or losing an election does not justify disobedience. The line is drawn where obedience would require sin.

Resistance: the views

Some Christians hold that believers may only refuse to obey sinful commands, never actively resist government. Others, in a long strand of Reformed thought, have argued that when rulers become tyrants, lesser magistrates — regional governors or parliaments — may lawfully resist them to protect the people. Some have gone further, justifying revolution by private citizens.

The New Testament pattern for individual Christians is refusal to sin, respectful speech and patient endurance, not violent rebellion. Christians may use lawful means to resist injustice: courts, elections, petitions and peaceful protest. Lawful authorities may have a duty to restrain a ruler who destroys justice. But private believers are never called to take up the sword against government on their own authority. “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19).

A conscientious objection

Think of a Christian nurse asked to take part directly in a procedure that ends a human life. She explains her conscientious objection respectfully to her manager, offers to care for other patients, and accepts that she may face consequences at work. She is not aggressive or self-righteous. But she will not do what God forbids.

Persecution

Jesus warned, “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you” (John 15:18). Paul told Timothy, “Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12). Across the world today, many Christians face imprisonment, violence and death for their faith. Believers in freer countries should pray for them, support them, and prepare their own hearts for whatever may come.

For reflection

Is there anything in your work or public life that would require you to disobey God? How would you respond respectfully and firmly? How does “but if not” shape your own faith?

4.title: Christians and Politics
4.essay:
Politics stirs strong feelings, and Christians are often divided by it. Scripture does not hand us a party manifesto, but it gives principles that should shape every believer’s engagement.

Justice matters to God

“Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people” (Proverbs 14:34). Nations are not neutral before God. He judges them as well as individuals. Christians who love their country will care about its righteousness, not only its prosperity or power.

God sent Jeremiah to the king’s palace with a message: “Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place” (Jeremiah 22:3). If the king obeyed, his dynasty would continue; if not, the palace would become a ruin. God holds rulers accountable for how they use power.

Micah sums up what God requires: “to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). The three belong together. Justice without kindness becomes harsh. Kindness without justice becomes weak. Both without humility become pride.

Some issues are clear

Scripture speaks plainly on some matters: the sanctity of human life from conception to natural death, the definition of marriage, honesty, the protection of the poor and vulnerable, and religious freedom. Christians should be clear on these.

Many are matters of wisdom

Many political questions, such as tax rates, economic policy, healthcare systems or immigration levels, involve how best to apply principles we share. Faithful Christians can and do disagree about them. Churches should not bind consciences where Scripture does not speak clearly.

Engagement without idolatry

Christians may vote, campaign, serve in office and speak publicly. But no party or candidate is the Messiah. When political identity becomes stronger than Christian identity, idolatry has crept in. Our hope is not in elections, but in Christ, whose kingdom will never end. A simple test: does your political identity shape your faith more than your faith shapes your politics?

Speech and civility

“Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6). Christians must speak truthfully and graciously about political opponents. Slander, mockery and outrage are no less sinful in politics than anywhere else.

Prophetic courage

John the Baptist rebuked King Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18). He was not campaigning for office. He was faithfully speaking God’s word to a ruler, and it cost him his life. Sometimes such courage is required.

The church and politics: the views

Some argue the church should actively campaign for political change and endorse candidates. Others argue it should be silent on public issues and focus only on personal salvation. Some hold that civil law should be based directly on the Old Testament law of Israel, a view called theonomy.

The church’s mission is to preach the gospel, make disciples and teach all that Christ commanded, including his moral law, which has public implications. Pulpits should proclaim clear biblical truth, but not endorse parties or candidates. Individual Christians, shaped by the church’s teaching, engage in public life as salt and light. The civil laws of Israel expired with Israel as a nation, though their underlying justice still instructs us.

Unity in the church

Christians of different political views must worship together as one body. The church is not a political party at prayer.

Think of two church members who support different parties and have argued bitterly online. Their pastor brings them together. They agree on the clear biblical issues, acknowledge that they differ on matters of wisdom, and commit to speak of each other, and of their opponents, with respect. They remain friends, and they pray together for their nation.

For reflection

Which political issues does Scripture speak to clearly, and which are matters of wisdom? How can you speak about political opponents in a way that honours Christ?

5.title: Salt, Light and Worldliness
5.essay:
Jesus did not tell his disciples to try to become salt and light. He told them they already were. The question is whether that presence is visible, and whether it has kept its saltiness.

You are

“You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:13–14). Salt preserves and flavours. Light exposes and guides. Christians are to be a preserving, flavouring and illuminating presence in society. “In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). A lamp hidden under a basket is useless. Good works, done openly and humbly, point people to the Father.

In the early centuries, when plagues struck Roman cities, many fled. Christians were often noted for staying to care for the sick, including pagans. Their conduct drew attention to their faith.

Losing saltiness

Jesus warned that salt which loses its taste is “no longer good for anything” (Matthew 5:13). Christians who become indistinguishable from the world lose their influence. The church’s power lies in its difference.

What worldliness is

“Do not love the world or the things in the world” (1 John 2:15). John names three ways the world captures the heart: “the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life” (1 John 2:16). And he adds, “the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17). Worldliness is investing in what will not last.

Worldliness is not enjoying creation, culture or good things. It is loving what the world loves in the way the world loves it: pleasure without God, possessions as identity, status as the goal of life. A Christian can be worldly in a monastery and godly in a marketplace.

It helps to notice that “the world” in Scripture can mean three things: the created order, which God made good; humanity, which God loves (John 3:16); or the system of human life organised in rebellion against God, which we must not love. Keeping these distinct helps us avoid both worldliness and unhealthy withdrawal.

Do not be conformed

After eleven chapters of gospel, Paul calls believers to offer their whole lives to God, and then warns, “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). The world presses us into its mould through media, advertising, education and peer pressure. The renewal of the mind comes through Scripture, prayer and Christian fellowship, and its fruit is the ability to discern God’s good and perfect will.

Engaging culture wisely

Christians can enjoy and create good art, music, literature and film, and can learn from the work of unbelievers, because all truth and beauty come from God. But we must also discern. In Athens, Paul’s “spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols” (Acts 17:16). Yet he quoted their own poets: “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28). We need both appreciation and discernment.

Christians have taken different approaches to culture: withdrawing from it, accommodating to it, or seeking to transform it. The New Testament calls for faithful presence: living distinctively within culture, contributing to its good, resisting its sin and pointing to Christ.

Freedom and love

In matters Scripture does not forbid — entertainment, food or drink in moderation — Christians have freedom. But that freedom is limited by love for weaker believers, and by the danger of being mastered: “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are helpful” (1 Corinthians 6:12), and “I will not be dominated by anything.”

Answer with gentleness

Peter writes to Christians facing suffering: “in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). Christians should be ready to explain their faith in public conversation, without arrogance or anger.

Think of a Christian student who is mocked for her faith in a philosophy class. Instead of becoming defensive, she listens carefully, asks thoughtful questions and, when invited, gently explains why she believes. Several classmates later ask to talk more. Her gentleness was as persuasive as her arguments.

For reflection

In what area of your life are you most conformed to the world? What would it look like to be transformed? Could you explain the hope that is in you in two minutes, with gentleness and respect?

6.title: Loving Our Neighbour and Seeking Justice
6.essay:
“And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). A lawyer asked Jesus this, hoping to limit his obligations. Jesus’ answer has been unsettling comfortable people ever since.

The good Samaritan

Jesus told of a man beaten and left half dead on the road. A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side. Then a Samaritan, a member of a despised group, stopped. He bandaged the man’s wounds, carried him to an inn and paid for his care.

Then Jesus turned the question around. Which of the three proved to be a neighbour? The lawyer answered, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said, “You go, and do likewise” (Luke 10:37). The question is no longer “Who is my neighbour?” but “Am I being a neighbour?” Our neighbour is anyone in need whom God places in our path.

Doing good to all

“And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:9–10). Christians care first for fellow believers, but not only for them. Doing good is not a single act but a lifelong habit, and it is never wasted.

The local church has a special responsibility to care for its own needy members, as the early church did for its widows (Acts 6; 1 Timothy 5). Individual Christians and Christian organisations can also serve the wider community.

Care for the vulnerable

“Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world” (James 1:27). True religion is both compassionate and holy, and neither can be neglected.

God has a special concern for the poor, the fatherless, the widow and the foreigner. “He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing” (Deuteronomy 10:18). Throughout Scripture, God’s people are called to reflect that concern.

Boaz, a wealthy landowner, let Ruth, a poor foreign widow, glean in his fields, and told his workers to leave extra grain for her (Ruth 2:15–16). He obeyed God’s law for the poor and went beyond it with kindness. His generosity became part of the story that led to David, and to Christ.

Speak up for the voiceless

A mother’s advice to her son, a king, includes this: “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy” (Proverbs 31:8–9). Power and influence are given to serve the vulnerable. Christians should speak for those who cannot speak for themselves: the unborn, the trafficked, the abused, the persecuted and the poor.

What justice is

Biblical justice means giving each person what is due under God’s law: protecting rights, punishing wrongdoing fairly, showing no partiality and caring for the vulnerable. It is defined by God’s character, not by any political ideology, left or right.

Loving enemies

Jesus calls us further still: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). That includes those who oppose us politically or attack us for our faith. Christian love is not limited to those who love us back.

Word and deed

Good works do not replace the gospel. People’s greatest need is to be reconciled to God. But mercy adorns the gospel and opens doors for it. Jesus healed and preached. The early church fed widows and proclaimed Christ. Word and deed belong together.

Think of a church that notices many refugees settling in its area. Members begin offering English classes, helping families find their way through local services, and inviting them into their homes. Some of the refugees become Christians. Others do not, but all have experienced Christ’s love through his people.

Our final hope

No human effort will bring perfect justice. “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14). Christians work for justice now, knowing it will always be imperfect, while waiting for the King who will judge the world in righteousness and make all things new.

For reflection

Who is the “wounded traveller” on your road, the person you are tempted to pass by on the other side? Who are the voiceless in your community that Christians should speak up for?
